# Iterated Local Search

A metaheuristic with exactly four moving parts: an **initial solution**, a **local search** that
descends to a local optimum, a **perturbation** that kicks the solution far enough to escape that
optimum but not so far as to restart, and an **acceptance criterion** deciding whether to keep the new
basin. Everything interesting is in the perturbation strength — too weak and it falls straight back
into the same optimum, too strong and it degenerates into random restart.

Unlike a genetic algorithm it carries no population, so there is no selection pressure and no
crossover; the entire search is one trajectory. That makes it cheap per iteration and easy to reason
about, and it is why the implementation in [[optimization-methods]] fits in one header and one source
file while the GA needs a parameter block.

## The concrete instantiation

Built for {{permutation-flow-shop-scheduling}} in `first_project`, minimising total flow time:

| Part | Choice |
|---|---|
| Initial solution | **NEH heuristic** — order jobs by descending total processing time, insert one at a time at the best position found so far |
| Local search | **1-shift insertion**, first-improvement — remove a job, reinsert it at every other position, take the first improving move |
| Perturbation | **Random swaps**, strength 4 |
| Restart | after `max(200, maxIter/5)` non-improving iterations |
| Stop | iteration budget, with an optional wall-clock cap |

Two details are worth pulling out because they are the ones that usually get skipped.

**First-improvement, not best-improvement.** The local search takes the first improving reinsertion
rather than scanning the whole neighbourhood for the best one. On a 500-job instance that difference
is the whole runtime budget.

**A stagnation restart on top of the perturbation.** Perturbation escapes a local optimum; the restart
escapes a *region* of local optima. Having both is what separates this from a simple
perturbation-loop, and the `max(200, maxIter/5)` floor means small budgets still get at least one
patience window rather than restarting constantly.

## Where it lands

ILS is one of the five racers in `first_project`, plotted in purple across all six convergence
figures. It was also the last method added, and the commit sequence is unusually legible for this
repo — `feat: add ILS interface` → `config: add ILS parameters` → `build: include ILS source file in
CMake target` → `feat: add ILS implementation with NEH init, insertion local search, and perturbation
loop` → `feat: integrate ILS runs and parameter sweeps in experiment runner`. Five commits, interface
before implementation, build wiring in the middle. That incremental shape is part of why
`first_project` reads as a genuine working log rather than an import — see
[[import-finished-work-into-git]].

Two of its parameters get their own sensitivity sweeps (`param_ilsMaxIter.png`,
`param_perturbStrength.png`), so the strength-4 choice is at least plotted even if the reasoning is
not written down.

## Relation to other local-search work

The same descend-then-escape structure appears in [[max-cut-and-local-search]] over in
[[discrete-mathematics-laboratories]], where a randomised local search is preferred to an exact
solver for the same reason: the neighbourhood is cheap and the exact method does not scale. The
[[multi-depot-vehicle-routing]] project a term later drops trajectory methods entirely for a
population GA, because there the hard sub-problem is a *partition* and crossover on the depot gene is
the lever that moves it.
